bp: The paper is about a common web problem: most useful knowledge is written for people, not stored for machines. A scientific paper, company manual, social post, scanned report, or slide deck may contain people, places, events, dates, claims, tables, diagrams, and source details, but they arrive as prose or layout rather than as clean facts. A web application that wants semantic search, grounded answering, or collaboration with large language models needs more than a pile of text. It needs a map of things and how they relate: which entity did what, when it happened, where it applies, what document supports it, and which other facts it touches. This tutorial serves that need by surveying how unstructured web content can be transformed into knowledge graphs. The point is not only storage. Once facts are structured, applications can retrieve by meaning, follow relations, check consistency, and give language models firmer evidence than raw passages alone.
wh: The hard part is that documents do not announce their structure in one simple form. A relation may be stated directly in a sentence, implied across several paragraphs, hidden in a table, shown by visual layout, tied to a time and place, or qualified by metadata such as author, source, section, or document type. A beginner might expect entity extraction to solve the problem: find names, find relation phrases, connect them. But web documents mix many kinds of evidence. Scientific papers have citations, figures, methods, and claims. Enterprise documents have headings, permissions, versions, and local terminology. Social posts have short context and loose language. Large language models can help read these sources, but they can also produce fluent facts that are not actually supported. Scale adds another tension: a system must process many documents while curating graph quality, factual consistency, multiple perspectives, and evaluation.
naive: A smart beginner would feed each document to a model and ask it to list entities and relations, then insert those pairs into a graph. For example, turn every sentence that says one thing affects another into a subject, relation, and object. That is sensible because a graph needs named things and links. It fails because documents contain more than simple pairs. Events have participants, times, places, and conditions. A table cell may depend on row and column headers. A visual layout can say that two blocks belong together. Metadata can decide whether a fact is trustworthy or current. The naive graph also has no strong way to merge duplicates, resolve conflicting facts, or prove that a generated relation came from the document rather than from model guesswork.
ap: The central move is to treat document-to-graph construction as a pipeline of evidence conversion and curation, not as a single extraction trick. The tutorial covers methods that first analyze documents across several dimensions: entities and relations, events, spatio-temporal indices, visual layouts, and metadata. Each dimension captures a different kind of structure that ordinary text search would flatten. Those pieces are then assembled into knowledge graphs that can support web applications. The graph is not just a bag of extracted triples. It must be curated for quality, built at scale, and shaped for multiple perspectives, because different users or applications may need different slices of the same document collection. The tutorial also emphasizes hybrid systems where large language models assist knowledge engineering, while structured knowledge grounds retrieval, reasoning, and generation. The core idea is mutual restraint: models help read messy documents, and graphs help keep model output organized and checkable.
mech: The mechanism begins with unstructured content: papers, enterprise files, posts, or other web documents. First, the system has to identify the document's internal pieces. Some pieces are textual, such as names, relation statements, events, claims, and definitions. Some are contextual, such as date, place, author, section, source, or document type. Some are visual, such as layout blocks, tables, figures, or spatial grouping on a page. Next, extraction methods turn these pieces into candidate graph material. Entities become nodes, relations become labeled links, events may become nodes or structured records with participants, and spatio-temporal information becomes indexable context. Metadata attaches provenance: which document or region supplied the fact. Then curation decides which candidates should survive. Duplicate entities must be merged, relation labels must be normalized, unsupported claims must be filtered, and conflicting perspectives may need to remain visible rather than be averaged away. At scale, this process must run repeatedly across many documents and keep graph quality from degrading as new content arrives. Finally, downstream systems use the graph. Search can retrieve by entity, relation, time, or topic. Retrieval-augmented answering can fetch graph-backed evidence from enterprise knowledge bases. Language models can use graph facts for grounded reasoning, while graph-building systems can use language models to propose extractions that are later checked.
math: The main mathematical object is a graph: a map made of nodes and links. A node stands for a thing, event, document fragment, place, time, or concept. A link says that two nodes have a specific relation, such as author-of, located-in, caused-by, cites, or mentioned-with. This matters because a relation is a constraint, not just decoration. If a document says an event happened in a city during a month, the event, place, and time restrict one another and can be searched together. Information extraction is a classification and matching problem: decide what span of text or region of a page refers to an entity, decide what relation is being expressed, and match repeated mentions to the same underlying thing. Ranking appears when many possible facts or retrieved graph pieces compete for attention. Probability appears because extraction evidence is uncertain; repeated patterns, source context, and model confidence can raise or lower trust. Curation is a consistency problem: choose graph edits that reduce contradictions and duplication while preserving useful disagreement. The tradeoff is compression versus detail. A graph makes documents computable by compressing prose, layout, and metadata into structured facts, but too much compression can erase qualifiers, uncertainty, visual context, or the exact wording that justified the fact.
dots: This paper sits directly in the repo's knowledge-graph family, where scattered facts must become connected evidence that can be followed, completed, updated, or protected. It also connects to the retrieval-augmented generation family. The local family data describes those systems as answer systems that should not rely only on what a language model already carries inside itself; this tutorial explains how the external evidence base can be built from documents in the first place. It touches information retrieval because semantic search needs more than keyword overlap: a query may need entities, relations, events, time, and provenance. It touches graph reasoning because extracted links let evidence travel through neighborhoods and paths. It touches evaluation and trust because the abstract names factual consistency, scalability, and evaluation as open challenges. Compared with papers that assume a graph already exists, this tutorial focuses on the upstream act of making the graph from messy web material.
ww: The approach works when it succeeds because it preserves structure that plain document search throws away. Raw text can tell a language model many things, but the model must hold them in a temporary context and infer the relations again each time. A curated graph stores the recurring structure once: these are the entities, these relations connect them, these events happened at these times, this source supports this claim, and this visual or metadata context changes how the claim should be read. That makes later search and reasoning more disciplined. A semantic search system can follow the relation that matters instead of matching a surface word. An enterprise question-answering system can fetch the connected evidence around a policy, product, or event rather than an isolated paragraph. A large language model can be grounded by graph facts and provenance, reducing the chance that fluent wording substitutes for supported evidence. The hybrid direction is especially natural because language models are useful readers of messy documents, while graphs are useful memory and checking structures. Each compensates for a weakness in the other.
po: The payoff is a systematic guide to building knowledge graphs from document collections for web applications. Participants are promised an overview of document analysis, document-to-graph methods, and hybrid systems combining large language models with structured knowledge. Practically, that supports semantic search, enterprise knowledge bases, grounded reasoning, and graph-augmented language-model workflows. The abstract also marks a field shift: knowledge graph construction is moving from mainly supervised deep learning models toward LLM-assisted knowledge engineering. The useful capability is not a single benchmark gain but a clearer construction path for turning messy web content into structured evidence that applications can search, reason over, curate, and evaluate.
limits: The input describes a tutorial, not a new evaluated system, so it does not prove that one construction method solves the named challenges. Its claims depend on whether documents contain enough recoverable structure, whether extraction methods can identify entities, relations, events, layout, time, place, and metadata accurately, and whether curation can keep quality high at scale. Large language models may assist extraction but can introduce unsupported facts unless checked against source evidence. Knowledge graphs can also become stale, overly rigid, or misleading when relation labels are wrong or conflicting perspectives are collapsed too early. The abstract names scalability, factual consistency, and evaluation as open challenges, so those remain assumptions rather than settled results.
